newsitem.title: USA: Dow falls 150 points as bond yields jump on rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Dow falls 150 points as bond yields jump on rate fears.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks plunged more than 150 points Monday to the lowest level since January, dragging down the dollar, as strong economic data reinforced fears the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again.
Bonds suffered smaller losses as the market's high yields attracted investors away from stocks. The dollar fell against major currencies.
In commodity markets, corn and soybean prices fell after a government report predicted larger plantings than had been expected.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 157.11 points, or 2.33 percent, to 6,583.48, a slide that was the sixth-largest in history in point terms and came on the heels of a 140-point skid Thursday, the last trading session before the Easter weekend. Financial markets were closed for Good Friday.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,138 to 538 on active volume of 555 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"There's clearly nervousness out there right now," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.

The stock market was hammered after new data showed the economy was still in high gear, which boosted the risk that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again in the months ahead. Last week, the Fed raised short-term interest rates by a quarter-point in an effort to keep the economy from overheating.

The government reported February personal income rose a higher-than-forecast 0.9 percent vs. a revised 0.4 percent increase the previous month, while consumption rose a smaller-than-expected 0.3 percent, compared with a revised 0.1 percent gain in January.
A sell-off in technology stocks and a weak showing by health-care stocks pulled the Nasdaq index down 27.81 points, or 2.23 percent, to 1,221.70.

In the bond market, the key 30-year Treasury bond slipped 4/32 of a point, or $1.25 on a $1,000 bond. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction of the price, rose to 7.10 percent from Thursday's close of 7.09 percent.

The rise in the bond's yield extended an upward creep that has become a pressing burden for stocks and has some questioning whether rates will level off anytime soon. Bond yields above 7 percent tend to draw money away from stocks and into bonds.

Wall Street will face a more important report Tuesday, when the National Association of Purchasing Management releases its March survey. The other important economic indicator due this week will be Friday's monthly payroll, wage and unemployment figures.

In currency markets, the dollar fell to 1.6750 German marks from 1.6800 marks at Thursday's close, after briefly touching a near two-month low of 1.6615 marks earlier. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar slid to 123.78 from 124.10 Thursday.
In commodities, prices for corn, soybeans and cotton to be harvested this fall sank after the government forecast larger plantings than expected
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for delivery in November closed 21 cents a bushel lower at $6.93. Corn for delivery in December ended down 5 cents a bushel at $2.91-1/2.
May soybeans closed up 3/4 cent a bushel at $8.55-3/4 and May corn at $3.10, up 1-3/4 cents.
Wheat prices closed lower on market talk that India cancelled a buying tender for 500,000 metric tons. Wheat for May delivery closed 4-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.97-1/2.
Overseas, European stock markets were closed for Easter Monday. In Japan, the 225-share Nikke average ended 1.02 percent or 186.32 points down at 18,003.40.
